cards.title: Hyperclique speedups for graph properties of fixed hardness
cards.formal: For every fixed integer h≥3, does the following implication hold? Assume that there exists δ∈(0,1) such that, for every fixed integer r≥h+1, an h-uniform hypergraph on N vertices can be tested for an r-vertex clique in worst-case time O(N^{r−δ}). Then, for every fixed k≥h and every fixed ∃ᵏ∀ graph sentence ψ of hardness H(ψ)=h defined below, is there an ε_ψ>0 and an algorithm deciding MC(ψ) in worst-case time O(m^{k−ε_ψ})? All algorithms in this statement are deterministic in the RAM model below. The premise assumes speedups for all clique sizes at one fixed hyperedge arity; it is not the unqualified assertion that these speedups exist.
cards.why: Would determine whether hyperclique detection exactly controls the algorithmic power needed at each structural hardness level of this expressive family of polynomial-time graph queries.
cards.status_note: Read the entire source question, its premise, the hardness definition, sparse partite model and preceding proposition. Checked the 2022 follow-up and full version, which distinguish their optimization result from this decision analogue. Later searches through 12 September 2026 found no proof or refutation of the stated universal implication. Searches are not exhaustive.

cards.definitions: The input to MC(ψ) is an explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with a partition V=X₁⊔⋯⊔X_k⊔Y. Every part is listed, may be empty, and edges join different parts. The fixed sentence is ψ=(∃x₁∈X₁)⋯(∃x_k∈X_k)(∀y∈Y)φ(x₁,…,x_k,y), where φ is a Boolean formula whose atoms are E(u,v) for distinct variable names u,v among x₁,…,x_k,y. E is symmetric adjacency; equality, extra relations and quantifier alternation inside φ are absent. A universal quantifier over empty Y is true and an existential quantifier over an empty X_i is false. The formula and k are fixed outside the input. Let m=1+|V|+|E|, counting vertex/part-membership records as well as edges; this makes the sparse input-size convention explicit and includes the cost of listed isolated vertices. To define hardness, set every atom E(x_i,x_j) to false in φ and replace E(x_i,y)=E(y,x_i) by z_i. The resulting Boolean function f:{0,1}ᵏ→{0,1} determines H(ψ). For a nonconstant f, H(f) is the largest t∈{0,…,k} such that, for every I⊆[k] of size k−t, there exists an assignment a∈{0,1}ᴵ for which the restricted function on the remaining t variables has exactly one falsifying assignment. Put H(f)=0 if f is constant, and H(ψ)=H(f). Thus the free coordinates must work for every choice of their set, but the pinned values may depend on that set. An h-uniform hypergraph has a finite vertex set and a set of unordered h-element hyperedges. An r-clique is a set of r distinct vertices every h-element subset of which is a hyperedge. The premise uses N, the number of hypergraph vertices, and an explicit adjacency table or list with polynomial-time conversion for fixed h. Use deterministic random-access machines with O(log L)-bit words for input-size parameter L, unit-cost arithmetic, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect access on a constant number of words; arbitrarily long integers do not have unit cost. In the premise L may be taken as N for fixed h,r; in the conclusion it is m. Input encodings use vertex numbers and explicit edges and parts. Machines are uniform in input size, with no length-dependent advice; a different fixed machine and multiplicative constant may be used for each fixed r or ψ. The same δ works for all r in the premise. ε_ψ and its constants may depend on h,ψ and the assumed speedup, but not on m. This common-δ reading retains the premise’s displayed exponent saving rather than replacing it by a single fast clique size.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication for every fixed h≥3, with a positive exponent saving for every fixed graph sentence of that hardness, or rigorously refute the implication. The known reverse-direction hardness result, an example of one easy sentence, or a speedup for only some sentences does not establish the universal conclusion. A theorem for optimizing the number of satisfying universal-variable choices under a different hardness parameter does not by itself answer the decision target.

cards.title: Constant-round distribution-free junta testing
cards.formal: Can distribution-free testing of k-juntas be performed in a constant number of adaptive query rounds using poly(k/ε) queries, with constants independent of the ambient dimension n? The tester must accept every k-junta and reject every Boolean function at distance at least ε from all k-juntas under an arbitrary unknown distribution, with success probability at least 2/3 in each case. The source recovers this target but leaves a material sampling convention unresolved: its function-query-only definition differs from the charged labeled-sample model used by its cited one-round lower bound. The completed benchmark must fix that convention before the round/query assertion is certified.
cards.why: The intended tradeoff asks how much sequential feedback is needed for dimension-independent testing under an unknown distribution, between polynomial adaptive complexity and an exponential nonadaptive lower bound in the charged-sample model.
cards.status_note: Read the conference and full versions and the cited lower-bound model. The missing ε is restored, but a fully self-contained round-complexity proposition needs the stated sampling conventions reconciled. Searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a later resolution or clarification. Recent junta testing for real-valued functions with approximate access concerns a different domain and oracle.

cards.review_note: The testing promise and desired O(1)-round, poly(k/ε)-query scale are recoverable, but the source does not reconcile its sample and round conventions with the lower bound it cites. Its Section 2.2 supplies unlabeled D samples and counts only queries to f, without a separate sample budget. The cited 2018 model charges labeled samples and membership queries together and calls an algorithm nonadaptive when its membership-query batch may depend on an earlier labeled-sample phase. A complete benchmark must decide whether unlabeled sampling is charged or bounded and whether sample labels contribute an adaptation phase. Imposing a polynomial total-oracle budget or permitting unbounded free samples changes the resource claim; no equivalence or author-supported choice was located.

sentences: The tester must distinguish a k-junta from a function ε-far from all k-juntas under an unknown distribution.
The source asks for constantly many adaptive rounds and polynomially many queries in k/ε, independently of n.
Fully adaptive algorithms already have almost-linear query complexity.
The cited exponential nonadaptive lower bound charges labeled samples, while the source’s own definition counts only function queries and provides unlabeled samples.
Sample accounting and the treatment of the preliminary sample phase must be reconciled before this becomes a complete benchmark.

cards.definitions: Let n≥1, 1≤k≤n and ε∈(0,1). A function f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} is a k-junta if some J⊆[n], |J|≤k, and g:{0,1}ᴶ→{0,1} satisfy f(x)=g(x_J) for every x. Let J_{n,k} be the class of all such functions. For a distribution D on {0,1}ⁿ, dist_D(f,J_{n,k})=min_{g∈J_{n,k}}Pr_{X∼D}[f(X)≠g(X)]. The target function and D are fixed before the randomized test. The source supplies a membership oracle returning f(x) on any chosen x and a sample oracle returning a fresh independent X∼D. The tester is given n,k,ε but no explicit description of D. It must accept if f∈J_{n,k}, reject if dist_D(f,J_{n,k})≥ε, and may behave arbitrarily between these cases. Probability is over its random bits and sample-oracle draws. Two-sided error is allowed; the separate one-sided question is not imposed here. In a batch of membership queries, all queried strings are chosen before any values from that batch are revealed; later batches may depend on earlier answers. A constant-round bound requires some fixed integer r independent of n,k,ε,f,D, and poly(k/ε) requires fixed C,b with worst-case charged cost at most C(k/ε)ᵇ. Which calls are charged and whether an initial labeled-sample phase counts toward r must still be fixed. Obtaining a label from the source’s unlabeled oracle requires a membership query. In contrast, the 2018 oracle returns (X,f(X)) directly, charges that sample and permits a nonadaptive membership batch to depend on all initial labeled samples. These conventions are explicitly distinguished; the card does not identify them without a resource-preserving argument. There is no requested bit-operation running-time bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Recover a consistent sample-cost and adaptation-round convention from the source question and its underlying testing model. Then establish or refute existence of fixed r,C,b achieving the displayed tester guarantees uniformly in n,k,ε. Until that convention is fixed, a polynomial bound counting only membership queries and a polynomial bound counting every labeled sample cannot be treated as the same answer. A uniform-distribution tester or a tester with a number of rounds growing with k does not answer the intended distribution-free constant-round question.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
